rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: NATO has a new plan to stop a Russian invasion of its eastern flank, and the core of it is AI-powered targeting and cheap drones. That is not a proposal — it's a codified strategy with a presentation date.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And nobody's calling it a robot army, which somehow makes it more serious.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: They've called it the Theory of Victory. I appreciate the confidence.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge. I'm Alex. With me are Jamie and Rufus. October fifth, twenty twenty-six — three stories, one connecting thread: AI changing the rules faster than the rules can keep up.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. When AI news moves this fast, knowing what happened is not enough; you need to know what changes your next decision. The Ledger turns the day’s noise into five focused briefings for people who need the consequence before consensus catches up. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So, the Theory of Victory. Bloomberg reported this in the last forty-eight hours. NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, has written an unclassified strategy document that formally integrates AI-powered targeting, low-cost drones, and minimally crewed systems into NATO's deterrence posture. He's presenting it in Poland on October twelfth.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Unclassified is doing a lot of work in that sentence. They're publishing the strategy but not the specifications.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. We know the broad shape — AI in the targeting loop, cheap drone swarms, smaller crews — but the actual model specs, the degree of human oversight in each decision, that stays unclassified in the vague sense.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: High level is the diplomatic word for it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What's the shift here, Rufus? Because NATO's been experimenting with drones since Ukraine in twenty twenty-two. What's new?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The formalization. Experiment becomes doctrine. There's a meaningful difference between a general saying "we've been watching Ukraine and drones are useful" and the Supreme Allied Commander circulating a document with a name and a presentation date. That's a signal to adversaries, to allies, and frankly to procurement offices.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That last one is probably the most consequential in the near term.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Almost certainly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The strategy draws explicitly on battlefield lessons since twenty twenty-two. What did Ukraine actually demonstrate that NATO is now trying to codify?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Cheap beats expensive at scale if you accept some attrition. A hundred-dollar drone that disrupts a tank column doesn't need to destroy the tank. It needs to slow the decision cycle. And AI in the targeting loop means you can process sensor data faster than a human commander can. The kill chain — sorry —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: the identification and response chain — compresses.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And that compression is the deterrent? The idea that NATO could respond so fast that the calculation for an invader becomes "we cannot actually win this quickly enough"?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's the explicit logic. The document reportedly aims to demonstrate readiness — to convince adversaries that victory is impossible before they begin.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, you flagged something before we recorded — the accountability question when the algorithm is in the loop.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Yes, and I want to push on this because it matters. If AI-powered targeting misidentifies something — a civilian convoy, an allied vehicle — who's accountable? The document is high-level. We don't know what "minimally crewed" means for the human in the loop. Does a human authorize every strike? Every tenth one?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The document doesn't specify, and that's not a small gap.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's the entire moral architecture of the system.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Is there a competing read on the risk here? Because I can construct an argument that faster, more accurate targeting actually reduces civilian harm compared to slower, more imprecise conventional artillery.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That argument works if the AI is reliably accurate. Ukraine showed drones can be jammed, spoofed, redirected. What happens when the AI is operating on corrupted sensor data?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Speed without accuracy is a very efficient way to make mistakes.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And NATO's own line is that this remains purely defensive.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is true until an invasion begins, at which point "defensive" and "highly lethal" are the same thing.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The deterrence theory only works if the adversary believes it. Which means NATO has to be able to demonstrate the capability credibly without actually using it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The October twelfth presentation in Poland is exactly that demonstration.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Poland is well chosen. It's the geography that matters. Eastern flank, close to the Suwalki Gap — the narrow corridor between Belarus and Kaliningrad that military planners have worried about for years. Presenting there is part of the message.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So the presentation is the deterrence. The document is the weapon.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Neatly put.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What should listeners watch for beyond October twelfth?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Defense procurement is the tell. "Minimally crewed systems" means a purchasing shift — fewer manned platforms, more autonomous or semi-autonomous ones. Watch which NATO member contracts expand in the next two quarters.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And watch whether the human-oversight question gets answered in the classified version or just quietly deferred.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Two weeks ago on this show we were discussing California's requirement for human review of AI-driven employment decisions. The logic isn't that different — what decisions does a person have to authorize, and when does speed make that authorization ceremonial?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I was going to let that connection pass, but you're right. The pressure against human-in-the-loop is almost identical. The AI works faster than the human can review.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The difference is that in employment law, the worst outcome is a wrongful termination. The stakes here are somewhat more irreversible.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the honest qualifier. What we don't know: exact specifications, oversight requirements, and what "demonstrating readiness" looks like in practice. What we do know: this is the first formally codified NATO doctrine built around AI targeting, it has a presentation date, and procurement will follow. Watch October twelfth. One thing the existing discussion hasn't settled — the document draws explicitly on lessons since the 2022 invasion. But Ukraine also showed that cheap drones get saturated. Defenders eventually run out of interceptors. Does the Theory of Victory account for that?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The saturation problem is exactly what "low-cost at scale" is meant to answer from the offensive side. The assumption is that if your drones are cheap enough, attrition is sustainable for you and unsustainable for the interceptor. The interceptor costs more than the drone.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which works until the adversary also has cheap drones in quantity.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: At which point you have a very efficient mutual degradation contest, yes.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And AI targeting in that environment — processing sensor data across hundreds of simultaneous contacts — is that where the human-oversight question gets most acute?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's where "every tenth authorization" stops being hypothetical and becomes operationally impossible. You cannot have a human reviewing individual targeting decisions when a hundred drones are active simultaneously.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The doctrine doesn't say it requires that. It also doesn't say it doesn't.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is the gap doing the work.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The document aims to convince adversaries that victory is impossible before they begin. But an adversary reading an unclassified document with no specifications —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: — is reading a press release with a presentation date.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So credibility still depends on something we're not seeing publicly.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's the oldest problem in deterrence, just running slightly faster now.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our second story. Norway has proposed a temporary ban on AI-powered glasses in specific public spaces — parks, beaches, schools, gyms, changing rooms. The government cited non-consensual recording as the primary concern and explicitly named Meta's Ray-Ban AI glasses. A parliamentary bill is being prepared.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The ban would not apply to private use where no risk to others exists.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Oslo schools had already banned smart glasses locally in late August. So this is the escalation from school policy to national law.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the editorial note that matters. This moved from institution-level to government-level within about six weeks.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is remarkable speed for a legislative body. Norway's digitalisation minister deserves some credit for not forming seventeen committees first.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: His name is Torgeir Micaelsen. And the move to form an expert group to draft permanent regulations suggests the temporary ban buys time for exactly that slower process.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the temporary ban is the committee, just with teeth.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Essentially.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The proposal's logic is that you cannot tell if someone wearing glasses is recording you. That's the core problem. Smartphones have a camera everyone can see. Glasses are invisible as a recording device.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Although — and I don't want to undercut the proposal entirely — smartphones in a gym changing room are already banned in most facilities. The enforcement is the same problem.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The difference is volume and passivity. You have to actively decide to hold up a phone. Glasses just record while you're looking around.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Fair. The decision friction is much lower.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us on location.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Picture a public park in Oslo — let's say Frogner Park, which is genuinely beautiful and presumably full of people who would prefer not to be quietly catalogued by a stranger's eyewear. The Norwegian government's concern, as Reuters reports it, is specifically the non-consensual recording of audio, video — and photographs in exactly this kind of ambient, everyday space. What's notable is that this is a geography-based approach to a hardware problem. The regulation follows the person's location rather than the device's capability. So the same glasses that are legal at home become illegal at the beach.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: But the glasses don't switch off when you cross into a park. You'd have to rely on the wearer choosing compliance.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Precisely the enforcement gap. Which is why the expert group drafting permanent regulations has a genuinely interesting technical question to answer — whether the regulation demands that devices have verifiable, tamper-evident indicators when recording, or simply prohibits entry. One of those is enforceable. The other is a norm with legal consequences.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story. Rufus flagged the enforcement gap. Jamie, is there a version of this that actually works?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I think the temporary ban works as a signal more than a mechanism. It tells the public: we see this as a rights issue, not just a tech etiquette issue. That has value even if enforcement is imperfect.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And it puts manufacturers on notice. If Norway passes this and two other Scandinavian countries follow, you have a regional standard that affects product design globally.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: There's a callback here. Three days ago we discussed Governor Newsom vetoing the California smart-glasses recording-indicator bill. His argument was essentially technical — that the bill as written was too broad. Norway is taking a different approach: ban first, design the permanent regulation second.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And California's veto is still unresolved as policy. Newsom said it needed more work, not that it was wrong. I'd want to see whether that bill comes back in the next session.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Meanwhile, Norway moves. The interesting question is whether the EU's broader AI Act framework absorbs this kind of proposal or whether member states retain the latitude to move faster.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Norway isn't an EU member — it's in the European Economic Area, so it has some regulatory independence here.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is why it can move quickly. Smaller government, clearer mandate.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And a genuine public consensus that privacy in physical spaces is worth protecting. That's not universal across jurisdictions.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What's the practical payoff for listeners? If you're traveling to Norway with Meta Ray-Bans, or if you build products in this space: the parliamentary timeline is the thing to watch. The bill hasn't passed. The proposal is real, the expert group is being formed — but "as soon as possible" in parliamentary language can mean a lot of things.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: In British parliamentary language it usually means next spring at the earliest.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Norway is not Britain.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: No, they have better fjords and apparently faster legislators.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing the Norway proposal doesn't answer — changing rooms and schools are obvious choices. But the draft specifically includes parks. What's the theory there? Parks are already public.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's exactly the distinction that matters. A park isn't a private space, but it's not a transactional space either. You're not consenting to documentation by being there. You're just — existing.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The Norwegian framing treats parks as spaces of reasonable anonymity, which is actually a fairly precise legal concept. You can be seen. You have not agreed to be catalogued.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Is that distinction enforceable, though? A tourist with a phone camera in Frogner Park is doing essentially the same thing.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Arguably, no. The phone requires a visible gesture. The glasses require only attention. That's not a trivial difference when the subject has no way to detect it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And the expert group they're forming has to answer this — whether the regulation targets the device or the behavior. Because if it's behavior, you need a different bill entirely.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: If it's the device, Meta's legal team is already drafting the challenge. If it's the behavior — non-consensual recording regardless of hardware — you've written something with considerably more durability.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And considerably more complexity to prosecute.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is why the temporary ban is doing the work of buying time. The permanent framework is the harder problem, and they're admitting that openly.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The admission is the most honest thing about the proposal. Most governments announce a framework and imply the details are settled. Norway has said: the details are not settled, here is time to settle them.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The private-use carve-out is also underexamined. The ban permits use in situations with no risk to others. Who determines risk?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's going to be the contested term in the parliamentary debate. "No risk to others" inside your own home is clear. "No risk to others" on a quiet street at seven in the morning is considerably less so.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The entire regulatory boundary lives in that phrase.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Rufus, another hundred AI headlines before breakfast? People have actual work to do. How do they decide what deserves their attention?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: With The Ledger, Jamie. A longer reading list is hardly a strategy. Five focused briefings help connect the news to decisions.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So The Ledger gives you a place to start asking better questions about your work and your team?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Precisely. The Ledger. Find the link in our show notes. Now, back to the discussion.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story is software security, and it's a concrete operational failure — not a hypothetical one. Google paused its open-source bug bounty program on October first. A bug bounty program is where companies pay independent security researchers to find and report flaws in their software. It's a genuinely important layer of protection for code that runs under the hood of applications enormous numbers of people and businesses rely on. Google paused this one because of a significant rise in automated submissions, and according to Google, the vast majority of those submissions were not valid.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So AI is being used to flood a security program with garbage reports.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the operational reality. And Google says it won't provide an update until Q1 of twenty twenty-seven — minimum three months.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Three months is an interesting number. Long enough to redesign intake. Short enough to suggest they have a plan rather than a crisis.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Or long enough to hope the problem quietly resolves itself, which seems optimistic given that the tools generating the garbage aren't going anywhere.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The irony is that AI tools were presumably adopted by researchers as productivity assistants — generate a report faster, submit more candidates. The individual incentive was entirely rational. The collective result was shutdown.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is the exact problem critics of automated code analysis have been raising for two years, so I want to ask — is this actually surprising to anyone?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The concern was theoretical. What's new is that it's happened at Google's scale, on a program that matters, with a concrete pause date and a Q1 return window. That's a different thing.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the volume question is telling even without Google's exact numbers. "Significant rise" plus "vast majority not valid" is the signature of AI-generated content applied to any intake system — high volume, near-zero quality filter.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's the same pattern as AI-generated scientific paper submissions, AI-generated legal discovery documents. The generation cost drops to nearly zero, so the incentive to check your work before submitting also drops to nearly zero.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: At zero marginal cost per submission, a report that's sixty percent right still has a non-trivial chance of a payout. Why not try?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the cost of sorting through all of it is borne entirely by Google's triage team, not the person who clicked submit.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the actual economic failure. The noise is free to generate and expensive to process, and those costs land on completely different people.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Classic commons problem. The shared resource — triage capacity — gets degraded by individually rational actors, none of whom bears the full cost of their own submission.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Is there a version of this where the pause is genuinely good news? Where Google comes back in Q1 with a better-designed system?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Possibly. If the new intake requires structured evidence — reproducible steps, affected code versions, something a model can't convincingly fake without actually finding a real flaw — then you've raised the bar in a way that serves everyone. The legitimate researcher can clear it. The speculative bulk submission can't.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I want that to be true. I just think three months is a long window for legitimate researchers who are effectively blocked from this channel in the meantime.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google pointed them to its other programs.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which don't cover open-source specifically. The overlap isn't complete, and the people who feel that gap most aren't Google's internal teams.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It's the independent maintainers. Someone writing open-source code who relied on this program for external security scrutiny of their work now has one fewer mechanism for that review — and no comparable substitute that Google is currently offering.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That consequence gets undercovered. It isn't just Google's intake process under pressure. It's the developers writing open-source software that millions of people use, who now have less external review, for at least three months.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: At minimum. Because Rufus's qualifier is the right one.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A Q1 update is not a Q1 resumption. The update could read: we need another quarter.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Worth holding onto. So what do security teams actually do with this? The practical implication is that if Google's program is being flooded, your own vulnerability disclosure channels face exactly the same pressure. The tools to generate a plausible-looking security report are available to anyone with an internet connection.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So teams that haven't already built quality filters into their submission process probably need to start — not because they're at Google's scale, but because the incentive structure is identical regardless of scale.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Require a proof of concept. Require a reproducible test case. Anything that costs the submitter effort proportional to the claim they're making. The bar just needs to be higher than zero.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The receipt on this one is specific: October first pause, Q1 twenty twenty-seven update. When Google comes back, watch what it publishes about changed submission requirements — because however it redesigns that intake will tell you how the rest of the industry is going to have to respond.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So we opened asking whether AI changes military deterrence or just adds new ways to escalate. Here's where we landed.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The honest uncertainty is whether speed in the decision loop makes the system more precise or just more efficient at making fast mistakes.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The procurement signal will tell you more than the presentation will. Watch which platforms get funded in the next two quarters.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Norway is proposing that AI glasses come off in public spaces — parks, schools, changing rooms. It's a geography-based approach to a hardware privacy problem, which is novel. The enforcement gap is real. The signal to manufacturers is also real. A parliamentary timeline is the thing to watch.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And the California veto from three days ago is still hanging. Two different regulatory approaches to the same problem, both unresolved.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google paused its open-source bug bounty program because AI-generated submissions overwhelmed its triage. The program covered flaws in software that underpins applications most of us use every day. It returns — maybe — in Q1 twenty twenty-seven. Security teams should read this as a preview for their own intake systems.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Same time. Slightly more drones.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The AI Edge. October fifth, twenty twenty-six. What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s question for you: If you saw someone wearing AI glasses in a public park, would you feel your privacy was being violated? Follow The AI Edge now. Join us tomorrow for what changes next.
